title: Continuous systems: feedback and block diagrams
subtitle: The analog-computer idea, made digital: wire integrators, gains and sums into a diagram and let it run.

sections.title: Analog computers and block diagrams
sections.body: Before digital machines, continuous models ran on analog computers: op-amp circuits wired as summers, gains and integrators, solving differential equations in real time. A hybrid computer paired analog parts with a digital controller. Modern continuous system simulation languages (CSSLs — Simulink, Modelica) keep the same picture: a block diagram of integrators, gains and sums. Below is the simulator built into this notebook.

sections.title: Turning an equation into a diagram
sections.body: Solve the highest derivative, then integrate down. For y′ + y = u: y′ = u − y, so a sum forms u − y, an integrator gives y, and a feedback wire returns y to the sum. The first-order system responds to a step by rising as 1 − e⁻ᵗ, with time constant 1 s.

worked.why: y′ + y = u, u = step(1). Rearranged y′ = u − y.
Steady state: y′ = 0, so y = u = 1. Time constant τ = 1: about 63% (0.632) at t = 1 and 98% near t = 4.

questions.prompt: Why is there a feedback wire from y back to the sum?

choices.text: Because y′ depends on y itself: y′ = u − y.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — y′ + y = u
figures.note: y′ = u − y, drawn as a loop.

sections.title: Second-order systems: oscillation
sections.body: A second-order plant 1/(s² + 2ζωₙs + ωₙ²) oscillates when the damping ratio ζ is less than 1. With ωₙ = 1 and ζ = 0.2 the step response overshoots by exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) ≈ 52.7%: the simulator gives 52.7% overshoot and settles at 0.9999. ζ = 1 is critical damping (fastest without overshoot); ζ > 1 is sluggish.

questions.prompt: The damping ratio ζ = 0.2 means the response is…

choices.text: Underdamped — it oscillates with noticeable overshoot.

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — ζ = 0.2

problems.prompt: For 1/(s² + 0.4s + 1) find the damping ratio and predicted overshoot. Then check it against the simulator.
problems.answer: 2ζωₙ = 0.4 with ωₙ = 1 → ζ = 0.2; overshoot = e^(−π·0.2/√0.96) = 52.7%. Simulator: 52.7%.

verify.caption: answer

sections.title: Feedback systems
sections.body: In a feedback control system the output is compared with a reference; the error drives a controller that drives the plant. With proportional gain K around the plant 1/(s+1) the closed loop settles at K/(1+K) of the reference: K = 2 gives 0.6667 — a permanent steady-state error. Adding integral action removes it: a PI controller (kp = 2, ki = 1) settles at 0.9999.

worked.why: Closed loop with gain K around 1/(s+1): y = K/(s+1+K) · r.
Final value for a unit step: K/(1+K). For K = 2: 2/3 ≈ 0.667.

questions.prompt: Why does proportional control alone leave a steady-state error?

choices.text: A non-zero output needs a non-zero error to keep the controller producing it.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Integral action accumulates the error until it vanishes.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Higher gain only reduces the error.

figures.caption: Figure 3.4.2 — PI control
figures.note: Integral action drives the error to zero.

sections.title: Nonlinear blocks and limits
sections.body: Actuators saturate, sensors have delays. Insert a saturation block: output clipped to ±1. A sine of amplitude 3 becomes a flattened wave — a first taste of distortion. Delays and saturation are why real systems need more care than their linear models.

choices.text: The output to a maximum and minimum value.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Beyond the limits the output stays flat.

figures.caption: Figure 3.5.1 — saturation
